Pochereth
pō′ker-eth
n. (a family of the servants of Solomon who returned from Babylon, further identified as "of Zebaim")
Hebrew Pokereth, feminine participle from pakhar, to catch, to snare; possibly an occupational name for a gazelle-catcher or fowler, joined to the place-name Zebaim.

Biblical Definition

Pochereth names a household counted among the children of Solomon’s servants: “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Ami” (Ezra 2:57), preserved at the same place in Nehemiah’s independent register: “The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Amon” (Nehemiah 7:59). The name is unusual among this whole list for carrying its own place-name attached, “of Zebaim,” likely marking the household’s town of origin before the exile, the only such double naming in this section of the register. The Hebrew root behind Pochereth suggests catching or snaring, possibly an ancestral trade of hunting or fowling, feminized in form, perhaps preserving an ancestress’s name at the head of the house rather than an ancestor’s. Whatever the household’s trade or origin, it is counted among those who “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), a trade-name and a town-name both carried home together.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Pochereth; the Hebrew root suggests catching or snaring, in a feminine form, joined to the place-name Zebaim, and belongs to a household of Solomon's servants who returned from Babylon.

expand to see more

POCHERETH, n. The head of a family of the servants of Solomon, called "of Zebaim," who returned from Babylonian captivity.

SNARE, n. A contrivance for catching an animal by entangling it.

CATCH, v.t. To seize, as with the hand; to lay hold on; to take captive.

FOWLER, n. A sportsman who pursues birds, or the occupation of taking birds.

NETHINIM, n. Those given; temple servants assigned to assist the Levites.

Key Scripture

Ezra 2:57 — "The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Ami."

Nehemiah 7:59 — "The children of Shephatiah, the children of Hattil, the children of Pochereth of Zebaim, the children of Amon."

Ezra 2:1 — "Now these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity, of those which had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away unto Babylon, and came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city;"

Nehemiah 7:73 — "So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities; and when the seventh month came, the children of Israel were in their cities."

Modern Corruption

A feminine-formed occupational name is a small, honest detail of the ancient record, not a doctrinal statement about women's roles one way or the other; it should not be pressed into service of a modern argument it was never meant to carry.

expand to see more

It would be an overreach in either direction to build a large theological argument on a single obscure genealogical name, whether to claim it proves matriarchal household leadership was normative in Israel or, conversely, to explain it away rather than simply noting the grammatical form honestly. The dictionary's complementarian conviction rests on the plain, repeated teaching of Scripture concerning the order of creation and the church, not on genealogical trivia, and this entry treats the name as exactly what it is: one household's inherited designation, feminine in form, of unknown further significance.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary dignity of a working household’s trade being remembered by name across a captivity and a return, whatever ancestor, man or woman, first bore it. The LORD’s record-keeping does not depend on the modern reader being able to reconstruct every detail of a family's internal history.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Pokereth, from pakhar, to catch, to snare; Tsevaim, the associated place-name; eved Shelomoh, servants of Solomon; golah (H1473), the exiled company.

expand to see more

Hebrew Pokereth — feminine participial form, from a root meaning to catch or snare.

Hebrew Tsevaim (Zebaim) — the place-name attached to this household, its likely town of origin.

Hebrew eved (H5650) — servant; the class-name behind “the servants of Solomon.”

Hebrew golah (H1473) — the exiled company; the census is a golah-register.

Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to return; the governing verb of the whole chapter.

Usage

"“The children of Pochereth of Zebaim” — the only doubly named household in this section."

"“Every one unto his city” — the resettlement the whole list records."

"“All Israel in their cities” — the closing summary of the return."
